native_result.query: In which domain do the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies with ratio of males in original and replication studies being and 0.87 and 0.84 respectively.
native_result.HypoB: In the replication-heterogeneity dataset, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies in the Economics domain. After excluding the 118 `drop==True` rows (all Social) and re-expressing the data with one ratio per unique O/R pair (using the project-published `aggregated==True` row for the 26 Many Labs multi-lab ids), Economics has mean authors_male.o = 0.87 (author-weighted 0.88; 77.8% of studies with ratio > 0.5) and mean authors_male.r = 0.84 (author-weighted 0.81; 72.2% of studies with ratio > 0.5) — above 0.5 on both sides for every aggregation we report. Social and Cognitive are majority-male on the original-paper side (means 0.66 and 0.71; weighted 0.64–0.71) but their replication-side central tendencies hover at or below 0.5 (study-level Social R mean 0.50, fraction > 0.5 = 48.4%; Cognitive R mean 0.52, fraction > 0.5 = 44.9%), so they do not satisfy the joint criterion. Economics has only n=18 O/R pairs (small sample), but the replication-side margin (~0.34 above 0.5) is large enough that the conclusion is unlikely to flip. The per-row sensitivity check (no id-collapse, 809 rows after drop filter) gives a consistent picture (Economics R mean 0.84, both Cognitive and Social R means < 0.55). File 2 (/meta-regression_replication_success_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv) does not contain discipline or authors_male columns and is not used in this analysis.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Load data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927x57) and verify schema — all 57 columns present and clean. 2) Drop the 118 rows where drop==True (all Social). 3) Collapse to one ratio per unique `id` (141 -> 131 ids after the drop filter). For the 26 Many Labs / multi-row ids, use the single aggregated==True row whose authors_male.r is the project-published study-level value. 4) For each discipline compute three central tendencies of authors_male.o and authors_male.r: unweighted mean across ids; author-weighted mean = sum(ratio * n_authors) / sum(n_authors); fraction of ids with ratio > 0.5. 5) Mark a discipline as 'majority-male' on side s iff all three aggregations exceed 0.5; the answer must clear both sides. 6) Sensitivity: repeat on the per-row data (no id-collapse). 7) Verify with the script artifacts/analysis.py — output also stored as artifacts/result.json.
